sentences.text: Nothronychus is a genus of therizinosaurid theropod dinosaurs named for its "slothful claw".
This bulky herbivore featured wide hips, four forward-facing toes, an elongated neck, and prominent arms ending in sharp claws.
The animal measured between 4.2 and 5.3 meters in length and weighed from 800 to 1200 kilograms.
Its large hands bore dexterous fingers equipped with curved, sharp claws that could reach up to 30 cm.
A long, S-shaped neck with small neural spines connected the head to the body, resembling the anatomy of ostriches and Diplodocus.
Studies of brain endocasts indicate Nothronychus had well-developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance useful for foraging.
Analysis of the braincase suggests Nothronychus had large pneumatic chambers optimized for receiving low-frequency sounds, possibly infrasound.
The type species Nothronychus mckinleyi was described by James Kirkland and Douglas G. Wolfe in 2001.
Nothronychus fossils were found near the New Mexico-Arizona border in the Zuni Basin within the Moreno Hill Formation.
The type species Nothronychus mckinleyi was discovered by James Ian Kirkland and Douglas G. Wolfe in 2001 in New Mexico, USA.
The Arizona Republic was the first to announce the discovery on June 19, 2001.
A second species, Nothronychus graffami, was described by Zanno and colleagues in 2009.
Researchers suggest Nothronychus was herbivorous, citing features like a keratinous beak, small skulls, and a large gut capacity.
Studies indicate Nothronychus hands were effective for piercing or pulling down vegetation to access food.
A 2024 study claims Nothronychus is herbivorous based on a retroverted pubis, suggesting this trait evolved multiple times in maniraptorans.
Nothronychus was exclusively or partially herbivorous, though it may have occasionally swallowed small vertebrates.
Research from 2015 identified three functional muscle groups at the neck base of Nothronychus: dorsiflexors, lateroflexors, and ventroflexors.
Nothronychus possessed an incipiently opisthopubic pelvis, which researchers associate with extensive modifications to its muscular system.
A 2023 study suggests Nothronychus walked with most motion occurring at the knee and limited movement at the femur.
Researchers suggest Nothronychus had a waddling gait and a digitigrade stance, though plantigrade walking remains a possibility.
While hearing estimates may be exaggerated, Nothronychus retained elongated semicircular canals associated with an active, predatory lifestyle.
Based on comparisons with Erlikosaurus, Nothronychus likely had a horizontal head posture enabling binocular vision.
Researchers believe the air sacs in Nothronychus supported an avian-style respiratory system rather than weight reduction or thermoregulation.
Nothronychus belongs to the theropod group Coelurosauria, which is mainly composed of carnivorous dinosaurs.
Nothronychus is part of the Maniraptora subgroup, a group of theropods that evolved into plant-eaters.
Nothronychus mckinleyi was assigned to the family Therizinosauridae in 2001 based on derived features.
Nothronychus lived during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Nothronychus fossils are found in the Moreno Hill Formation, an environment characterized by tectonic upheaval, volcanic activity, and a humid climate.
Nothronychus lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 92 to 91 million years ago in the Turonian stage.
Nothronychus lived 90 million years ago in swampy forests similar to modern swamps in Louisiana.
Nothronychus coexisted with the ceratopsian Zuniceratops and some small theropods.
There is debate regarding the phylogenetic position of Nothronychus, with some analyses placing it basally while others suggest the fossil record is too limited for reliable determination.
